name: Yonghe Qiang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sims, Nathaniel Aaron. 2017. The Suprasegmental Phonology of Yonghe Qiang in Typological Perspective. MA thesis, University of California, Santa Barbara. eScholarship qt9c24v9v0 (public PDF, 62 pp.).
catalog_locator: Sec. 3.7 'Accent in Yonghe', pp. 15-16; sec. 4.2.1, p. 24; sec. 4.2.3, pp. 25-26; sec. 5.4, p. 53.
catalog_quote: In Yonghe, accent is obligatory, culminative, and lexically specified. [...] I use the term 'accent' as opposed to 'stress' for three different reasons. First, accent placement is lexically specified and the relevant domain is the word rather than the syllable. Second, while accent is culminative at the level of the phonological word, some compounds consist of two (or multiple) phonological words and thus may contain two (or more) accents. Third, 'stress' generally refers to relative prominence, however, as will be discussed below, Yonghe accent is not strictly an issue of relative prominence as it is obligatory even for monosyllabic forms in isolation. [...] In the Yonghe variety, non-prominent (unaccented) vowels are subject to gradient devoicing. [p. 24] The high-initial forms are toneless trochees, and are represented as /*Ø-Ø/. [...] The high-final forms are analyzed as toneless iambs. For these forms, the high pitch on the second syllable is the realization of the iambic accent, while the low pitch on the syllable can be explained as the default realization of Ø as low in unaccented position. Words of this type are represented as /Ø-*Ø/. [p. 53] An examination of accent-type frequency reveals that iambs and trochees are equally distributed, although there is a slight tendency towards iambicity.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every phonological word carries exactly one obligatory accent (realised as high pitch, greater duration and amplitude; unaccented vowels are devoiced or reduced), and its position is lexically specified: simplex disyllabic nouns are either trochees (high-initial) or iambs (high-final, the most frequent pattern), and a privative /L/ tone on the accented syllable gives a third, rising-initial melody. Accent placement is also morphological in verbs (accent on the directional prefix = prohibitive). The 2021 dissertation reframes the system as tonal (pitch patterns high-initial = trochaic, high-final with prominence 'difficult to say', rising-final = iambic) and says the 2017 accent analysis 'has issues', so the accent-vs-tone framing is unsettled, but no source gives a positional stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; accent is culminative per phonological word, though compounds made of two phonological words can carry two accents (p. 16); compounds show deaccentuation and tone sandhi (ch. 5).
new_statements.exceptions: Simplex nouns with [L-LH] are unattested (left-to-right tone association, p. 27); final rises occur only in morphologically complex forms; compound accent/tone alternations are partly unpredictable (p. 35); Sims 2021 p. 151 finds it 'difficult to say which syllable is more prominent' in high-final disyllables (first syllable longer, second higher in pitch and intensity).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (defined pp. 13-14 by rhotic harmony and play-language domain); data are isolated-word and carrier-sentence recordings of nouns from Ka'er village, Yonghe Township (two speakers), plus elicited verbs; Sims 2021 ch. 3 covers monosyllables, disyllables and Sichuanese loans.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Yonghe variety (Glottolog dialect yong1287; Ka'er village, Yonghe Township, southeastern Mao County), one of the two dialects Glottolog 5.3 groups under sout3257 'Southeast Maoxian Qiang'; the other dialect, Goukou (gouk1234), has no description. Sims 2016 established the 'SE Maoxian' group (Yonghe + Goukou) as belonging to neither Northern nor Southern Qiang. The earlier scan's 'Sims 2016 (LTBA)' is actually Language and Linguistics 17(3) and is open access.

sources.note: Sec. 3.7 'Accent in Yonghe' (pp. 15-16): accent is obligatory, culminative and lexically specified; placement is lexical, domain is the word; unaccented vowels are devoiced/reduced. Sec. 4.2 (pp. 23-27): simplex disyllables are toneless trochees /*Ø-Ø/ (high-initial), toneless iambs /Ø-*Ø/ (high-final, 'the most common pattern for disyllabic forms', p. 21) or /*L-Ø/ (accented L realised as rising); accent shift to the directional prefix marks prohibitive (pp. 25-26). Ch. 5: compounds show deaccentuation and tone sandhi.

sources.quote: The subgroup-internal evidence comes from regular correspondences between tonal varieties. These data allow us to put forward a working hypothesis that proto-Rma had a two-way tonal contrast. Furthermore, existing accounts of how tonogenesis occurred in the tonal varieties are shown to be problematic.
sources.note: Re-examines the tonogenesis hypothesis for Rma (Liu 1998, Evans 2001) and argues instead that tone or its phonetic precursors were present in proto-Rma; regular correspondences between the tonal varieties (Yonghe among them) support a working hypothesis of a two-way tonal contrast in proto-Rma, corroborated by tonal correspondences with Prinmi and Tangut. Per the Sims 2021 dissertation's summary of this paper, Yonghe's two-way (privative /L/ vs toneless) contrast reflects loss of PTB consonant codas: smooth syllables > high pitch patterns, checked (*-p *-t *-k) syllables > low-rising patterns.
